title: Biggest and smallest number from twenty four sticks
description: An example, the biggest number and the smallest number are made with exactly twenty four sticks. The biggest comes from the cheapest digit used as often as possible, and the smallest from the fewest digits with the smallest digit first. Keeko raises the doubt that the biggest digits make the biggest number.
teaching_notes: One idea: more digits make a bigger number, so the cheapest digit gives the biggest number and the fewest digits give the smallest. Watch for students who pick the biggest digits instead of counting digits first.

source: Make a number using exactly 24 sticks. Find the biggest and the smallest such numbers.
video_script.why: The child can count the sticks in a number, and now chooses digits for a fixed number of sticks to make the biggest and the smallest number.
video_script.substitution: More digits make a bigger number; use the cheapest digit for the biggest, and the fewest digits with the smallest first digit for the smallest.
video_script.anchor: digits drawn with sticks, with a box of exactly 24 sticks beside them
video_script.wrong_answer: the biggest digits make the biggest number
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko picks the biggest digit, nine, four times, without noticing that a number with more digits is bigger.
video_script.payoff_line: More digits make a bigger number, and fewer digits make a smaller one

final_answer.spoken: twelve ones in a row for the biggest, and two thousand eight for the smallest

maths_rules: biggest: each digit needs at least 2 sticks, so at most 24 / 2 = 12 digits, and 12 digits at 2 sticks each are all 1s: 1,11,11,11,11,111 (twelve ones)
smallest: three digits hold at most 3 x 7 = 21 sticks, under 24, so four digits are needed
first digit: 1 uses 2 and leaves 22, more than 21 that three digits hold; 2 uses 5 and leaves 19 = 6 + 6 + 7, so 2, 0, 0, 8
the slip: 9, 9, 9, 9 use 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24 sticks and make 9999, but it has only four digits
video_script.design: One idea: more digits make a bigger number. The stick digits stay in the anchor; the working band builds the example, then the biggest, then the smallest. Keeko's doubt: the biggest digits make the biggest number.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Remember, one takes two sticks, two takes five, zero takes six and eight takes seven.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, build an example.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Two, zero, zero and eight take five, six, six and seven sticks.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>That makes exactly twenty four, so two thousand eight is one example.

marks.m2: each digit needs at least 2 sticks, and 1 needs exactly 2, is written
marks.m4: twelve 1s are drawn, each with 2 sticks

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, the biggest number needs the most digits.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Each digit needs at least two sticks, and the digit one needs exactly two.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Twenty four divided by two is twelve, so at most twelve digits fit.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>Twelve digits use two sticks each, so every digit is a one.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>The biggest number is twelve ones in a row.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, the smallest number needs the fewest digits.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Three digits take at most twenty one sticks, with all eights.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>That is under twenty four, so we need four digits.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, choose the digits from the left.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A one leaves twenty two sticks, and three digits hold only twenty one.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A two leaves nineteen sticks, and zero, zero and eight use exactly nineteen.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The smallest number is two thousand eight.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>More digits make a bigger number, and fewer digits make a smaller one.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>The biggest is twelve ones in a row, and the smallest is two thousand eight.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Two thousand eight is also our example.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks the biggest digits make the biggest number.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Nine takes six sticks, so four nines use exactly twenty four.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>That makes a number with four digits, nine thousand nine hundred ninety nine.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>But twelve ones make a number with twelve digits.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>More digits beat bigger digits, so twelve ones are far bigger.
